In mathematics, the '''Voorhoeve index''' is a non-negative [[real number]] associated with certain [[Function (mathematics)|functions]] on the [[complex number]]s, named after [[Marc Voorhoeve]]. It may be used to extend [[Rolle's theorem]] from real functions to complex functions, taking the role that for real functions is played by the number of zeros of the function in an [[interval (mathematics)|interval]].

==Definition==
The Voorhoeve index <math>V_I(f)</math> of a complex-valued function ''f'' that is [[analytic function|analytic]] in a complex [[Neighbourhood (mathematics)|neighbourhood]] of the real interval <math>I</math>&nbsp;=&nbsp;[''a'',&nbsp;''b''] is given by

<math display="block">V_I(f) = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_a^b \! \left| \frac{d}{dt} {\rm Arg} \, f(t) \right| \,\, dt \, = \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_a^b \! \left| {\rm Im}\left(\frac{f'}{f}\right) \right| \, dt. </math>

(Different authors use different normalization factors.)

==Rolle's theorem==
[[Rolle's theorem]] states that if <math>f</math> is a [[continuously differentiable function|continuously differentiable]] real-valued function on the [[real line]], and <math>f(a)=</math> <math>f(b)=0</math>, where <math>a<b</math>, then its derivative <math>f'</math> has a zero strictly between <math>a</math> and <math>b</math>. Or, more generally, if <math>N_I(f)</math> denotes the number of zeros of the continuously differentiable function <math>f</math> on the interval <math>I</math>, then <math>N_I(f) \le N_I(f')+1.</math>

Now one has the analogue of Rolle's theorem:

<math display="block">V_I(f) \le V_I (f') + \frac12.</math>

This leads to bounds on the number of zeros of an analytic function in a complex region.
